newsitem.title: UK: Widow fighting for husband's sperm sparks debate.
newsitem.headline: Widow fighting for husband's sperm sparks debate.

text.p: A British woman's fight to have a baby using her dead husband's sperm has split doctors grappling with the moral dilemmas of modern medicine.
The 30-year-old woman, whose husband died last year from bacterial meningitis, has mortgaged her house to pay for the 80,000 pound ($125,000) case that comes to court in London on Wednesday.
"I didn't lose the ability to have his child and that is still there. That is what I'm fighting for. I want the rest of my life back," said the woman, who is making British legal history.
The woman, who has not been named, told BBC Television: "Really what it boils down to is that me and my husband had a life planned. We had decided exactly what we wanted."
The sperm was taken from the man at her request whilst he was on a life support machine in a coma. They had been trying for a year to have a baby.
The Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority refused permission for her artifical insemination, saying the law would be broken as she did not have her husband's written consent.
Doctors picking their way through an ethical maze of life and death decisions, expressed sympathy for the woman but were sharply divided on how they felt the case should go.
Dr Stella Lowry, spokeswoman for the British Medical Association, said: "We understand completely that she has effectively got the consent of her husband."
But she added: "We also recognise that the law was created to make sure that doctors make the right medical use of the new technologies available."
But John Parsons, conception unity consultant at King's College Hospital in London, said the woman's move was macabre. "One has to have clear-cut rules about this sort of thing," he said.
About 18,000 women a year are treated at British fertility clinics. There are an estimated 1,500 frozen embryos created in test-tube baby clinics that are unwanted by their parents.

The Embryology Authority provoked an uproar earlier this year when it ordered the destruction of thousands of human foetuses created by in-vitro fertilisation because they had passed a legal deadline.

The risks of fertility treatment were graphically highlighted on Monday night. A woman expecting octuplets lost three of the babies after being admitted to a London Hospital when only about 20 weeks pregnant.
Doctors treating Mandy Allwood warned that the outlook for the other babies was bleak. They fear they cannot save any of them by caesarian operation until the pregnancy reaches its 24th week.
